name: Ubongo: educational cartoons for children in Africa (charityevals' estimate)
beneficiaries_note: Our build: Ubongo publishes no audience split by country; weighted to Tanzania, where it began and broadcasts most, then Kenya and Nigeria (its largest other markets) and the other countries whose languages it dubs into (Kinyarwanda, Chichewa and others), a judgment.
summary: Ubongo makes educational cartoons for TV, radio and online in Africa: Akili and Me for children of 3-6 (early literacy, numeracy, English, emotions) and Ubongo Kids for 7-14 (maths and science), broadcast free in about 22 countries; its US arm spent 7.2 million dollars in 2024 and Ubongo counts 42 million households reached a month, so the cost per child is a few cents. Children in poor countries who watch Sesame Street's local versions at home learn about a fifth of a standard deviation more than those who don't (Ubongo's own trials point the same way), and we value that as higher adult earnings after cutting it for occasional viewers, survey and small-study bias, repeat years of viewing and fade-out. That gives about {{result}} years of healthy life per 1,000 dollars, but the result is mostly uncertainty (plausible range about 8 to 270): the size of the home-viewing effect, how much of it lasts into adult earnings, and whether the audience counts are right drive it. The whole programme is discounted for missing data, as no study measures Ubongo's home audience in standard deviations.

Households reached each month (TV, radio and online)

source.title: Ubongo, Strategic Plan 2024-2028
source.quote: Currently reaching 42 million households monthly on TV, radio and digital in 12 languages and 22 countries

rows.explainer: Ubongo's own count from media ratings and household surveys in its markets (p. 10: character recognition 'measured through nationally representative household surveys'), as of 2024. The plan also says 'By 2024, we have reached 42 million kids' (p. 21), so the unit is loose; an earlier Ubongo fact sheet says media ratings show its content 'regularly viewed and listened to by over 24 million learners' (https://www.ubongo.org/wp-content/uploads/Reach_popup.pdf), the low end. High 50 million for growth since. Ubongo's count, not an independent one: the doubt about who really watches is in implementation_adj.

rows.label: Average household size
rows.explainer: The site's household sizes for Ubongo's three largest markets (Tanzania, Kenya, Nigeria), about {{row:household_size}} people; Tanzania's figure is the rural one, the only one the site has. Households with a television are more often urban and smaller, so this is a little high.

rows.label: Share of household members aged 3-14 (the shows' audience)

source.title: World Bank, World Development Indicators: population ages 0-14 (% of total), 2024
source.quote: Tanzania 42.5, Kenya 36.8, Nigeria 41.0 (per cent of the population aged 0-14)

rows.explainer: About 40% of people in Tanzania, Kenya and Nigeria are 0-14 (World Bank, 2024); ages 3-14, the ages of Akili and Me (3-6) and Ubongo Kids (7-14), are about four fifths of that in a young population: 31%. Low 27% for urban, television-owning households with fewer children; high 34%.

rows.label: Share of children aged 3-14 in a reached household who watch or listen
rows.explainer: Judgment 50% (30-80%): Ubongo counts households, and not every child in a household that tunes in watches: some are at school when the shows air, some are too old for Akili and Me or too young for Ubongo Kids. Anchor: the result, about 0.7 children per household, against Ubongo's own 'reached 42 million kids' (p. 21), which would be 1 per household; low end for the earlier 24 million 'regular' learners.

rows.label: Children aged 3-14 who watch or listen in a month
rows.explainer: About 28 million children, counted as one year's audience against one year's cost.

rows.label: Learning gain of a child who watches regularly at home (standard deviations)

source.title: Mares & Pan (2013), Effects of Sesame Street: a meta-analysis of children's learning in 15 countries, Journal of Applied Developmental Psychology 34:140-151, doi:10.1016/j.appdev.2013.01.001 (open copy)
source.quote: The average effect estimate for surveys conducted in low- and middle-income countries was significant and positive (d = .213, SE = .070, 95% confidence interval = .076-.351, z = 3.04).

rows.explainer: Viewers against non-viewers (or heavy against light viewers) of a broadcast season of Sesame Street's local co-productions, in the six surveys in low- and middle-income countries where children chose to watch at home (29 estimates, 5,967 children): the audience Ubongo counts, watching as they choose. Studies where children were shown the programme find more (cognitive outcomes 0.284, 0.165-0.403, Table 4), a check that the home figure isn't high. For 7-14-year-olds, Watson, Hennessy and Vignoles find Tanzanian children who watch Ubongo Kids score higher in maths within the same household (Uwezo survey, about 39,000 children; a coefficient of 0.126, SE 0.035, on a maths scale with SD 0.84, so about 0.15 SD by our division; the thesis states 0.106 SD, the coefficient multiplied by the SD; British Journal of Educational Technology 52(2), 2021, thesis version https://api.repository.cam.ac.uk/server/api/core/bitstreams/33899038-0e39-4e0b-bb42-6588456cae64/content, PDF p. 169, printed p. 165), cross-sectional, so a check only. Ubongo's own trials find the same direction without standard deviations to pool: four weeks of daily Akili and Me improved Tanzanian pre-schoolers' scores on five of seven outcomes against children shown other programmes (Borzekowski 2018, Journal of Applied Developmental Psychology 54:53-59), a Rwanda trial on eight of ten (Borzekowski and others 2019, International Journal of Early Childhood 51:109-126, https://eric.ed.gov/?id=EJ1215041), while a northern Nigeria study found 'no differences associated with study's initial group assignments' (Borzekowski and others 2023, https://www.ubongo.org/wp-content/uploads/Akili-and-Me-and-the-COVID-19-shutdown-1.pdf, p. 1). Those doubts are in evidence_adj.

rows.label: A year of viewing's gain relative to the studies' first exposure
rows.explainer: Judgment 60% (30-100%): the audience is counted every year, and a child watches Akili and Me for about four years (ages 3-6) and Ubongo Kids for up to eight; the surveys compare children after a season of viewing, often their first, and later years repeat some of what was learnt (letters and counting once known). Low 30% if most of the gain comes in the first year of several; 100% if each year's new episodes teach as much as the first.

rows.label: Share of the learning gain still there in adult life
rows.explainer: The site's one figure for low- and middle-income countries (@education.test_gain_persistence_to_adulthood: {{row:learning_persistence}}, 20-70%): test gains fade between the programme and adult work.

rows.label: Adult earnings gain per SD of skill held as an adult
rows.explainer: The site's one figure for low- and middle-income countries (@education.earnings_gain_per_sd_adult_skills_lmic: {{row:earnings_gain_per_sd}}, 10-30%), per SD of reading and maths skill still there in adult life, so it multiplies the persisting share above. A cross-check: Kearney and Levine find more exposure to Sesame Street raised US children's chance of being at the right grade for their age (3.2 points for a 30-point rise in coverage) and a wage effect near the edge of significance (NBER w21229, pp. 24 and 28, https://www.nber.org/system/files/working_papers/w21229/w21229.pdf).

rows.label: Years from viewing to adult earnings
rows.explainer: Judgment 12 years (8-16): Akili and Me's viewers are 3-6 and start earning at about 16-20, 14 years on; Ubongo Kids' are 7-14, about 9 years on. Anchor: GiveWell's 8 years for school-age children dewormed (@givewell_shared.years_until_income_benefits_deworming), whose children are older than Akili and Me's.

rows.label: Years the earnings gain lasts
rows.explainer: The shared figure (@givewell_shared.long_term_benefit_years), as in every model of later income.

rows.label: Household members who share the earnings gain
rows.explainer: The shared figure (@givewell_shared.resource_sharing_multiplier): the earner's household shares the extra income, as in the later-income rows of every model.

rows.label: Consumption per person a year in Kenya, for reading (2021 PPP dollars)
rows.explainer: For reading only: the gain below is a share of the viewer's future earnings, so no baseline enters it. Kenya's household-survey mean, one of Ubongo's main markets, gives the scale: a 0.1% gain on it is about a dollar a year.

rows.label: Gain in ln(consumption) per child, over working life, discounted to today
rows.formula: ln(1 + effect_sd * repeat_year_ratio * learning_persistence * earnings_gain_per_sd) * pv_annuity_due(1, $discount_rate, working_years) * (1 + $discount_rate) ^ (0 - years_until_work) * resource_sharing_multiplier
rows.explainer: ln(1 + learning gain × share for a year of viewing × share lasting into adult life × earnings per SD) in each working year, discounted at the shared rate, after the wait until work, shared with the household. Before the adjustments below.

rows.label: Learning by caregivers and others outside the counted audience, as a share of the children's benefit
rows.explainer: A side effect, judgment 5% (0-20%): children over 14 and adults in the household watch too, and Ubongo makes parenting content for caregivers; no study measures what they gain, so it is counted small. Anchor: kept small enough that its range moves the result by under a fifth.

rows.label: Mortality benefits as a share of the earnings benefit
rows.explainer: 0 (0-2%): Akili and Me teaches handwashing and healthy habits (a before-after study found children's health knowledge rose, Kauffman and others 2022, https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC9140413/), but no study links the shows to deaths averted; the health knowledge is counted in unmodelled_benefits_adj.

rows.label: Evidence adjustment (internal and external validity)
rows.explainer: 0.55 (0.3-0.85), internal × external. Internal 0.6: the home-viewing estimate comes from surveys, where children who choose to watch may differ from those who don't; the meta-analysis's studies are small, tested on what the show taught (letters, counting), and small education studies find about three times the effect of large ones (Evans and Yuan 2022, https://doi.org/10.3102/01623737221079646); Ubongo's Nigeria study found no difference by assignment. External 0.9: Sesame Street's co-productions are, like Ubongo's shows, local-language curricula broadcast free in poor countries; Ubongo's own trials point the same way. Fade-out before adult life is in the shared persistence figure, not here. Anchor: charityevals' Save the Children education branch (0.6 for the same small-study bias).

rows.label: Share of counted child viewers who watch regularly, like the surveys' viewers
rows.explainer: Judgment 55% (30-80%): a household counts if it tuned in during the month, while the surveys' viewers watched a broadcast season. Anchor: Ubongo's fact sheet counted 'over 24 million learners' who view or listen regularly, from media ratings of about 2021 (https://www.ubongo.org/wp-content/uploads/Reach_popup.pdf), against the 42 million monthly of 2024, a ratio of 0.57 across years. Gains rise with engagement: in Ubongo's Nigeria study each Akili and Me character a child could name went with about 3% higher literacy and numeracy scores (Borzekowski and others 2023, Table 2, p. 10), so occasional viewers gain less.

rows.label: Share of the outcome that wouldn't have happened anyway
rows.explainer: 90% (70-100%): the studies' effects are against children watching other programmes or none, so another channel's cartoons are already netted out; a little educational content (other local or dubbed shows) would fill some of the airtime without Ubongo.

rows.label: Ubongo International's share of the Ubongo group's spending
rows.explainer: Judgment 85% (60-100%): the audience is reached by the whole Ubongo group (Ubongo International in the US, Ubongo Learning in Tanzania, offices in Kenya and Rwanda); the US return funds its sister organisations with grants ($3.5 million in 2024), but they also take some grants and earn some content and licensing income of their own, which no published account totals. Low 60% if the African entities raise a large share themselves.

rows.label: Ubongo's share of the resources behind the broadcasts (against broadcasters' and partners' own)
rows.explainer: Judgment 70% (40-100%), Convention 2: over 60 TV and radio stations carry the shows, free to viewers (Strategic Plan, p. 21; Reach_popup.pdf); Ubongo publishes no airtime terms, and its return shows only $103,139 of advertising and $1.59 million of programme service fees, which may include airtime bought. Where stations give the airtime, its value counts on the partners' side; partners who run screenings and hand out toolkits give their own time too. 70% if partners' airtime and time are worth about 40% of Ubongo's own spending; 100% if Ubongo pays for all the airtime; 40% if donated airtime is worth one and a half times its spending.

rows.label: This charity's share of the resources behind the outcome
rows.explainer: Ubongo International's share of the group's spending × the group's share of everyone's resources behind the broadcasts.

rows.label: Share of credit used
rows.explainer: The charity's share of the resources behind the outcome; it applies whichever way credit is shared.

rows.label: Leverage and funging
rows.explainer: 0.85 (0.6-1.0): in 2024 Ubongo International raised $29.1 million in grants against $7.2 million of spending, and its net assets rose from $10.1 million to $32.0 million (Form 990, Part I lines 8, 18, 20-22), largely multi-year grants for the 2024-28 plan, whose five-year fundraising goal was $28 million (Strategic Plan, p. 31). With the plan largely funded, part of a new gift is money its large funders would have given anyway.

rows.label: Cash at the end of 2024

source.title: Ubongo International, Form 990 for 2024 (IRS e-file, via ProPublica Nonprofit Explorer)
source.page: Part X lines 1 and 2, column B
source.quote: Cash non-interest-bearing 11,480,602; savings and temporary cash investments 286,133

rows.explainer: Cash and savings at the year end; pledged grants not yet received are left out, as they aren't money waiting to be spent. Investment income was $6,351 (Part VIII), too little to grow the waiting money.

rows.label: Years a gift waits before it is spent
rows.explainer: Cash at the year end over a year's spending, about {{row:gift_to_grant_years}} years.

rows.label: Discount for the wait before a gift is spent
rows.explainer: The wait discounted at the shared rate; the wait from viewing to adult earnings is in ln_gain_per_person.

rows.label: Counted less where the outcome isn't measured for this charity
rows.explainer: Thin (the shared missing-data step): Ubongo's household count, with an effect from Sesame Street's studies (other delivery); Ubongo's own trials publish no standard deviations to pool, and its largest home-viewing study is cross-sectional.

rows.label: All adjustments combined
rows.formula: evidence_adj * counterfactual_adj * attribution_share * implementation_adj * leverage_funging_adj * wait_discount * missing_data_adj
rows.explainer: The product of the adjustments above.

rows.label: Benefits and harms not modelled, as a share of modelled value
rows.explainer: A side effect, judgment +5% (-10% to +20%): social-emotional and health learning (Akili and Me's lessons on emotions and handwashing; Kauffman and others 2022 found gains in both, before-after only) beyond what earnings capture, +10%; less the time a child spends in front of a screen instead of playing, reading or being read to, which observational studies link to slower early development, -5%. The low end lets the harm outweigh.
